title: Why Data Quality Matters in Machine Learning
text:
A machine-learning model can only learn from the data it receives. If that data contains errors, incorrect labels, or inaccurate measurements, the model’s predictions and the conclusions drawn from it may be affected.
A study published in Scientific Reports on 11 October 2026 examined how different types of data errors influence machine-learning performance and the interpretation of important features.

title: Why Data Quality Matters in Machine Learning
text:
Why This Matters
Data scientists often spend considerable time selecting algorithms and improving model accuracy. However, this research highlights why the quality of the input data also deserves attention.
For example, incorrect entries in a healthcare dataset could affect predictions about patient outcomes. Similarly, errors in financial data could influence a model used to assess risk.
It is therefore important to note that building a good model involves more than choosing an algorithm, data cleaning, validation, and understanding how data was collected are also essential parts of a reliable analysis.
Source: Scientific Reports — Data Science research.

text:
If you are learning data science, you do not need complicated algorithms or huge datasets to begin building a portfolio. Start with a clear question, a manageable dataset, and an analysis you can explain.
Here are five beginner-friendly projects to try in 2026.

title: 5 Data Science Projects Beginners Can Build in 2026
text:
If you are learning data science, you do not need complicated algorithms or huge datasets to begin building a portfolio. Start with a clear question, a manageable dataset, and an analysis you can explain.
Here are five beginner-friendly projects to try in 2026.

title: 5 Data Science Projects Beginners Can Build in 2026
text:
1. Student Performance Analysis
Explore how study time, attendance, and other factors relate to students’ academic performance.
Skills: Data cleaning, exploratory data analysis, visualisation.
Dataset: UCI Student Performance.

title: 5 Data Science Projects Beginners Can Build in 2026
text:
2. Personal Expense Analysis
Analyse spending by category and month to identify where money goes and which expenses take up the largest share.
Skills: Data cleaning, grouping, summary statistics, charts.
Dataset: Create a small spreadsheet of sample expenses or use a public financial dataset.

title: 5 Data Science Projects Beginners Can Build in 2026
text:
3. Weather Trend Analysis
Investigate temperature or rainfall patterns over time. Identify the hottest months, compare seasons, and visualise changes.
Skills: Time-series analysis, data visualisation, descriptive statistics.
Dataset: Open-Meteo historical weather data.

title: 5 Data Science Projects Beginners Can Build in 2026
text:
4. Wine Quality Prediction
Explore whether chemical measurements, such as acidity and alcohol content, are associated with wine quality.
Skills: Correlation, regression or classification, model evaluation.
Dataset: UCI Wine Quality.

title: 5 Data Science Projects Beginners Can Build in 2026
text:
5. A Simple Data Dashboard
Choose a small sales or survey dataset and create a dashboard showing important totals, comparisons, and trends.
Skills: Data analysis, visualisation, communicating insights.
Tools: Excel, Power BI, Tableau, or R.

title: 5 Data Science Projects Beginners Can Build in 2026
section: How to make your project stand out
text:
How to make your project stand out
Do not stop at copying a tutorial. Write down a question, clean and explore the data, create meaningful charts, explain your findings, and document your code on GitHub.
Three well-finished projects that demonstrate your thinking are more useful than many unfinished projects.
The important thing is to start small, answer a real question, and build on what you learn. The goal is to demonstrate that you can turn data into understandable, useful insights.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
Fuel efficiency is an important consideration in vehicle design because it affects fuel costs and the amount of fuel consumed during travel. Understanding how vehicle characteristics relate to fuel efficiency can help explain differences in the performance of cars.
This analysis uses the built-in mtcars dataset in R to investigate the relationship between fuel efficiency, vehicle weight, and engine horsepower.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
Fuel efficiency is an important consideration in vehicle design because it affects fuel costs and the amount of fuel consumed during travel. Understanding how vehicle characteristics relate to fuel efficiency can help explain differences in the performance of cars.
This analysis uses the built-in mtcars dataset in R to investigate the relationship between fuel efficiency, vehicle weight, and engine horsepower.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
2. Objectives
The objectives of this analysis are to:

Describe fuel efficiency in the selected vehicles.
Examine the relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency.
investigate whether vehicle weight and horsepower are associated with fuel efficiency when considered together.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
3. Dataset description
The mtcars dataset contains observations on 32 automobiles and 11 variables. The data were extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine and describe cars from the 1973–1974 model years.
The variables used in this analysis are:

MPG: Fuel efficiency, measured in miles per US gallon.
Weight (wt): Vehicle weight, measured in thousands of pounds.
Horsepower (hp): Engine horsepower.

The dataset is included with R, so no external file or download is required.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
4. Exploratory analysis
The next step to take is to examine whether vehicle weight is associated with fuel efficiency. The scatter plot below displays the relationship between vehicle weight and miles per gallon.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle Weight and Fuel Efficiency",
    x = "Vehicle weight (thousands of pounds)",
    y = "Fuel efficiency (miles per US gallon)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 1: Relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency in the mtcars dataset.





As shown in Figure Figure 1, the relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency appears negative. Heavier vehicles generally have lower miles-per-gallon values, while lighter vehicles tend to have higher values. The fitted line summarizes the overall linear trend, and the shaded region represents its confidence interval.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
5. Statistical modelling
A multiple linear regression model is used to investigate the association between vehicle weight, horsepower, and fuel efficiency.
The model is expressed as:
[ MPG_i = _0 + _1 WT_i + _2 HP_i + _i ]
where (MPG_i) represents fuel efficiency, (WT_i) represents vehicle weight, (HP_i) represents horsepower, and (_i) represents the error term.

model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)

summary(model)

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
6. Results
The regression coefficients and their statistical significance are presented in Table Table 1.

model_results <- as.data.frame(summary(model)$coefficients)

model_results$Variable <- rownames(model_results)
rownames(model_results) <- NULL

  "Variable", "Estimate", "Std. Error", "t value", "Pr(>|t|)"
)]

A negative regression coefficient indicates that an increase in the predictor is associated with lower fuel efficiency, after accounting for the other variable in the model. A positive coefficient would indicate the opposite direction.
The p-values provide evidence about whether each coefficient differs from zero under the assumptions of the fitted model. They should be interpreted alongside the estimated effect sizes and the limitations of the dataset.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency in Cars
text:
7. Conclusion
The exploratory plot and regression model provide two complementary ways of studying fuel efficiency. The plot makes the relationship between weight and miles per gallon easy to see, while the regression model estimates the associations of weight and horsepower with fuel efficiency simultaneously.
These results describe associations rather than proving that vehicle weight or horsepower causes a change in fuel efficiency. Other factors, including engine technology, vehicle design, and driving conditions, are not accounted for in this simple model.
The dataset is also relatively small and represents automobiles from the 1970s. Its results should therefore not be treated as representative of modern vehicles.
